titre: The Zoroastrian Tower of Silence, Suspended by the Disappearance of the Vultures
accroche: Between 1993 and 2002, Indian vultures declined by more than 97%: the only funeral rite that depends on a wild animal was left without an executor.
contenu_vulgarise:
In Mumbai, on Malabar Hill, the Parsis (descendants of the Zoroastrians who fled Iran after the Arab conquest) still lay their dead on the flat roof of a circular tower, open to the sky, so that birds can finish the body. The rite is called dakhma, “tower of silence” in its English equivalent. This is not a folkloric detail: it is the only solution compatible with a doctrine that absolutely forbids touching the three sacred elements of Zoroastrianism.

## A Corpse With Nowhere to Go

The religion founded by Zoroaster regards the dead body as inhabited by a demon of pollution, Nasu, which contaminates everything it touches. Yet earth, fire, and water are sacred: one can therefore neither bury, burn, nor immerse a corpse without defiling one of the three. Only air remains, and the scavengers found in it. Exposure does not make pollution vanish by miracle: it entrusts it to vultures, the only creatures able to make flesh disappear without any sacred element coming into contact with it.

The practice is ancient. In the 5th century BCE, Herodotus already notes, in his *Histories* (I, 140), that among the Persians a man's body is buried only after it has been torn by a bird or a dog, before being coated with wax and put in the ground: an in-between arrangement less strict than the later practice, since the earth ends up receiving the body. Stone towers proper appear in the sources only much later: the Middle Persian term dakhmag is attested only in Zoroastrian texts of the 9th–10th centuries, and the first structures identified as such date to the early 9th century. Between Herodotus and the towers of Mumbai, the doctrine has not changed; its implementation has.

## What This Changes

This system has a single point of failure: the vultures themselves. In the 1990s, a cheap anti-inflammatory, diclofenac, came into general use in Indian livestock farming to relieve sick cattle. Vultures that feed on the carcasses of these animals die of kidney failure within a few days. The study that establishes the link, published in *Nature* in 2004 from Pakistani colonies, came two years before India banned veterinary diclofenac, in 2006: too late for the bird population: between 1993 and 2002 already, the Indian vulture and the slender-billed vulture had dropped by 97.4%, the white-rumped vulture by 99.7%.

A rite built never to depend on a human decision (not the fire one lights, not the pit one digs, only birds doing what they have always done) found itself without an executor for a reason entirely external to the religion: a molecule used on cows. The Parsi community of Mumbai tried solar concentrators to speed up decomposition, then began breeding vultures in captivity; some now resign themselves to burial or cremation, the two solutions the doctrine had precisely ruled out. The pollution no longer comes from the corpse: it comes from whatever killed the bird meant to take care of it.

repere.texte: Between 1993 and 2002, the Indian vulture (Gyps indicus) and the slender-billed vulture (Gyps tenuirostris) dropped by 97.4%, the white-rumped vulture (Gyps bengalensis) by 99.7%, poisoned by diclofenac given to livestock: the very species on which the completion of the Zoroastrian funeral rite depended.
repere.source: Swan, G. E. et al., “Toxicity of diclofenac to Gyps vultures,” Biology Letters, vol. 2, no. 2, 2006, pp. 279–282, cited by Wikipedia (English), “Indian vulture crisis”

carte.punch: A religious rite comes to a halt: not because a doctrine changes, but because a bird dies.
carte.idee: Zoroastrianism forbids delivering a corpse to earth, fire, or water, all three sacred: only exposure to vultures respects the rule. From the 1990s on, an anti-inflammatory given to livestock caused their population to fall by more than 97%, leaving the rite without an executor.
carte.source_courte: Swan et al., 2006; Herodotus, Histories, I, 140

quiz.question: Why can't Zoroastrianism replace exposure to vultures with burial or cremation?
choix: Because earth, fire, and water are sacred, and a corpse would defile all three
Because Indian law forbids burial and cremation to religious minorities
Because Zoroastrians regard vultures as deities that must be fed
Because the body must remain visible so that the living can pay homage to it
quiz.explication: The doctrine forbids polluting the three sacred elements; no law imposes this choice, vultures have no divine status, and exposure aims at decomposition without contact with earth, fire, or water, not at the visibility of the body.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Herodotus report about the treatment of the body among the Persians?
choix: The body is burned at once, on a pyre built in the open air
The body is immersed in a river, then left to the fish
The body is torn by a bird or a dog, then coated with wax and put in the ground
The body is exposed on a stone tower until it decomposes
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In Herodotus, the earth ends up receiving the body: it is an in-between arrangement less strict than the later practice, and stone towers appear only much later.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why did Indian vultures nearly disappear starting in the 1990s?
choix: An avian epidemic ravaged the colonies of the subcontinent
They were dying of kidney failure after eating the carcasses of cattle treated with diclofenac
The Parsis drove them away to prevent pollution of the towers
India banned their presence over large cities
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Diclofenac, a veterinary anti-inflammatory, kills vultures through kidney failure within a few days; India banned it only in 2006, when the population had already collapsed.
